entry: Public research university in [[Bologna]], [[Italy]], and the oldest university in continuous operation in the world. Teaching began around 1088, and by the late 12th century students had organized into guilds (*universitates scholarium*) that hired scholars to teach them. Its motto, *Alma Mater Studiorum*, is [[Latin]] for "nourishing mother of studies." The university has over 90,000 students, one of the largest universities in Europe. It educated Nicholas Copernicus during the Renaissance, and alumni include Italian scientists, prime ministers and judges. Campuses in Cesena, Forlì, Ravenna and Rimini complement the main site, with branches in [[Buenos Aires]], New York, [[Brussels]] and [[Shanghai]]. It also houses botanical gardens, museums and archaeological collections.

Public land-grant research university in Berkeley, California, founded in 1868 as the state's first land-grant university and the founding campus of the University of California system. It is named after the Anglo-Irish philosopher [[George Berkeley]]. The university is organized into fifteen schools, including the College of Chemistry, the College of Engineering and the Haas School of Business, and it enrolls more than 45,000 students. It manages the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory for the U.S. Department of Energy. Berkeley was a founding member of the Association of American Universities and one of the original eight Public Ivy schools. Its alumni, faculty and researchers include 65 Nobel laureates.

Public land-grant research university in the Westwood neighborhood of [[Los Angeles]], California, and the second-oldest campus in the University of California system after [[University of California, Berkeley|Berkeley]]. Its academic roots date to 1881, and it became independent of Berkeley on June 14, 1951. The university offers 337 undergraduate and graduate degree programs and received 174,914 undergraduate applications for Fall 2022, the most of any university in the United States. Its student-athletes, the Bruins, have won 126 NCAA team championships, second only to [[Stanford University]]. Affiliates include 19 Nobel laureates, seven [[Pulitzer Prize]] winners and 10 astronauts.

Collegiate public research university in [[Cambridge]], England, founded in 1209 by scholars who left the [[University of Oxford]] after a dispute with local townspeople. It is the second-oldest university in the English-speaking world and the third-oldest in continuous operation. The university comprises 31 semi-autonomous colleges and more than 150 departments and institutions. Its press, Cambridge University Press and Assessment, is the oldest university press in the world. Undergraduate teaching centers on weekly small-group supervisions in the colleges. The university operates eight museums, including the Fitzwilliam Museum, and its 116 libraries hold about 16 million books. Alumni include King [[Charles III]], [[Isaac Newton]], [[Charles Darwin]] and [[Alan Turing]], and its alumni, academics and affiliates have won 126 [[Nobel Prize|Nobel Prizes]].

Private research university in the Hyde Park neighborhood of [[Chicago]], Illinois, incorporated in 1890 with donations from [[John D. Rockefeller]]. It has an undergraduate college, four graduate research divisions and seven professional schools, plus centers in [[London]], [[Paris]], [[Beijing]] and [[Delhi]]. The Metallurgical Laboratory produced the world's first human-made, self-sustaining nuclear reaction, in Chicago Pile-1 beneath Stagg Field. Its scholars helped establish the Chicago schools of thought in economics and sociology. The University of Chicago Press is the largest university press in North America, and its students, faculty and staff have included 102 Nobel laureates.

Public research university in [[Copenhagen]], Denmark, founded in 1479 and the second-oldest university in [[Scandinavia]], after Uppsala University. Its first four faculties were [[Theology|theology]], law, medicine and [[Philosophy|philosophy]]. The university was dissolved about 1531 amid the spread of Protestantism and re-established in 1537 by King Christian III. It now has six faculties, 36 departments and 122 research centers across four campuses in Copenhagen, and it operates two research stations in [[Greenland]]. As of October 2022, 10 Nobel laureates and one Turing Award laureate had been affiliated with the university. Alumni include one president of the United Nations General Assembly and at least 37 prime ministers of Denmark.

Public research university in Göttingen, [[Lower Saxony]], [[Germany]], founded in 1734 by the Electorate of Hanover's government on the orders of George II. It began admitting students in 1737 and is the oldest university in Lower Saxony. [[Napoleon]] called it "the University of Europe." Between the late 19th and early 20th centuries it was a major center for mathematics and physics, where [[David Hilbert]], Felix Klein and [[Max Born]] conducted influential research. Its international student body included [[J. Robert Oppenheimer]]. Adolf Hitler's rise to power in 1933 led to the dismissal or emigration of numerous faculty, including many of Jewish origin or those opposed to the regime. The university reopened in 1945 in British-occupied Germany. It is affiliated with 47 [[Nobel Prize]] winners by its own count and is a member of the U15 group of German research universities.

Collegiate research university in [[Oxford]], England, with evidence of teaching as early as 1096. It is the oldest university in the English-speaking world and the second-oldest in continuous operation. Growth accelerated after 1167, when [[Henry II of England|King Henry II]] barred English students from the University of Paris. After conflict with Oxford townspeople, some academics fled to Cambridge, establishing the [[University of Cambridge]] in 1209. It has 43 colleges but no main campus; its buildings are scattered through the city. It operates the Ashmolean Museum, the world's oldest university museum, and Oxford University Press, the largest university press in the world. Its alumni include 31 prime ministers of the U.K., and as of October 2025, 76 Nobel laureates and four [[Fields Medal|Fields Medalists]] had been affiliated with it.

Private [[Ivy League]] research university in [[Philadelphia]], Pennsylvania, chartered in 1755 by its first president, [[Benjamin Franklin]]. It is one of nine colonial colleges in the United States. Its medical school was the first in North America, and its law school's first professor, James Wilson, helped write the U.S. Constitution. In fiscal year 2024 the university reported $2.172 billion in research expenditures, second among U.S. universities. Its endowment was $31.1 billion as of June 30, 2026. Its alumni, trustees and faculty include eight signers of the Declaration of Independence and three U.S. presidents.

Public research university in Bunkyō, [[Tokyo]], Japan, founded in 1877 as the nation's first modern university by merging several older institutions. Its precursors date from the [[Edo period]] and include the Tenmongata, founded in 1684 as the astronomical research arm of the [[Tokugawa shogunate]], and the Shōheizaka Institute, a Confucian school. The university was chartered on April 12, 1877, by the [[Meiji Restoration|Meiji]] government with four faculties: law, science, letters and medicine. It has 10 faculties, 15 graduate schools and 11 affiliated research institutes. As of 2023 it enrolled 13,974 undergraduate and 14,258 graduate students. Its land holdings total 326 sq km, among the largest landowners in Japan. As of 2025 its alumni and faculty include 17 prime ministers of Japan, 22 [[Nobel Prize|Nobel Prize]] laureates, seven astronauts and a [[Fields Medal|Fields Medalist]]. Its alumni have founded major companies, including [[Toyota]] and Hitachi.

Public research university in the Greater Toronto Area of [[Ontario]], Canada, founded by royal charter in 1827 as King's College. It was the first institution of higher learning in Upper Canada and was initially controlled by the [[Church of England]]. It became a secular institution and took its present name in 1850. Its three campuses, St. George, Mississauga and Scarborough, enroll more than 100,000 students, making it the largest post-secondary institution in Canada. It has over 720,000 alumni and is the birthplace of [[Insulin|insulin]], [[Stem cell|stem cell research]] and the first artificial cardiac pacemaker. It is also associated with the development of [[Deep learning|deep learning]] and the identification of the first black hole, [[Cygnus X-1]]. A CA$250 million donation from James and Louise Temerty in 2020 was the largest philanthropic gift in Canadian history.

Public research university in [[Vienna]], Austria, founded on March 12, 1365, by Rudolf IV, Duke of Austria. It is the oldest university in the German-speaking world and one of the oldest in continuous operation. In 1551 Emperor Ferdinand I installed the [[Jesuits]] at the university, and in the mid-18th century [[Maria Theresa]] placed it under the control of the monarchy. It grew into the largest university in the Holy Roman Empire and, during the [[Humanism|advent of Humanism]] in the mid-15th century, had more than 6,000 students. As of 2024–2025 it offered 185 degree programs, and it has about 85,000 students and 11,000 employees. It is associated with 17 [[Nobel Prize|Nobel Prize]] laureates. Its scholars include [[Erwin Schrödinger]], [[Karl Popper]] and [[Sigmund Freud]].

Family of multitasking, multi-user [[Operating system|operating systems]] that derive from the original AT&T Unix. Development began in 1969 at [[Bell Labs]] by Ken Thompson, [[Dennis Ritchie]] and others. It was the first portable operating system, almost entirely written in the [[C (programming language)|C programming language]] from 1973. Its modular design follows the Unix philosophy, in which small tools each perform one well-defined function and are combined through pipes and the Unix shell. Version 7, released in 1979, was the last widely distributed Research Unix. Vendors including Microsoft, Sun Microsystems and [[IBM]] produced variants, and the University of California, Berkeley developed BSD. Until 2005 Unix was the most widely used server operating system, and [[Linux]] and GNU have since eclipsed it in popularity. Commercial Unix systems such as IBM AIX and Oracle Solaris remain in use in certain fields.

Date and time representation widely used in computing, measuring the number of non-leap seconds since 00:00:00 [[Coordinated Universal Time|UTC]] on 1 January 1970, the Unix epoch. For example, midnight on 1 January 2010 was Unix time 1262304000. Unix time originated as the system time of [[Unix]] operating systems and is now used in other operating systems, [[File system|file systems]], [[Programming language|programming languages]] and [[Database|databases]]. In Unix time each day has exactly 86,400 seconds, so the count ignores [[Leap second|leap seconds]], which cause a discontinuity when they occur. Values are typically stored as signed integers, sometimes at higher granularity such as microseconds.

[[Aircraft]] with no human pilot, crew or passengers on board, operated autonomously or by remote control. Also called a drone, it is part of an unmanned aircraft system (UAS) that includes ground controllers and communications links. Developed through the 20th century for [[Military|military]] missions too "dull, dirty or dangerous" for humans, they were essential to most militaries by the 21st century. As control technologies improved and costs fell, their use expanded to many non-military applications, including aerial photography, [[Agriculture|precision agriculture]], forest fire monitoring, product deliveries and drone racing. The [[United States Department of Defense]] and the Federal Aviation Administration adopted the term UAS in 2005. Autonomous drones employ computer vision, [[Machine learning|machine learning]] and [[Deep learning|deep learning]] to carry out missions without human intervention.

Hypothetical [[Chemical element|chemical element]] with atomic number 119, symbol Uue, also called eka-francium. It is expected to be an [[Alkali metal|alkali metal]], the first element of the eighth period, and the lightest element not yet synthesized. Attempts have been ongoing since 2018 at RIKEN in Japan, and since 2026 at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research in Dubna, Russia. Relativistic effects may make it less reactive than [[Caesium|caesium]] and [[Francium|francium]], closer to [[Potassium|potassium]] or [[Rubidium|rubidium]]. It is also predicted to show +3 and +5 oxidation states, which are unknown in any other alkali metal.

Ancient [[Sanskrit]] religious and philosophical texts of [[Hinduism]], the most recent part of the [[Vedas]]. They deal with [[Meditation|meditation]], philosophy, consciousness and ontological knowledge, and they document the transition from the archaic ritualism of the Veda into new religious ideas. Of 108 known Upanishads, the first dozen or so are the oldest and most important, and the principal texts are believed to predate the [[Common Era]]. Their central concern is the relation between ritual, the cosmos and the human person, postulating [[Brahman]] and Ātman as the summit of a hierarchically arranged, interconnected universe. Their varied ideas shaped later traditions such as [[Vedanta]], and the German philosopher [[Arthur Schopenhauer]] called them the most profitable and elevating reading possible in the world.

Third and last subdivision of the [[Paleolithic]], or Old Stone Age, dating roughly from 50,000 to 12,000 years ago. It ends with the start of the [[Holocene]] and is followed by the [[Mesolithic]]. *Homo sapiens* emerged in Africa around 300,000 years ago, but marked increases in artifact diversity came after about 50,000 years ago. The period has the earliest known evidence of organized settlements, and its artists produced [[Cave painting|cave paintings]], carvings and engravings on bone or ivory. [[Cro-Magnon|Cro-Magnons]] in Europe left sophisticated stone tools, while [[Neanderthal|Neanderthals]] kept using Mousterian technology. Hunting was important, and caribou or wild reindeer may be the species of greatest importance to studies of hunting. The [[Last Glacial Maximum]] divides the period, and the [[Peopling of the Americas|peopling of the Americas]] occurred during it.

Highest [[Social class|social class]] in modern societies, made up of the [[Wealth|wealthiest]] members and those with the greatest political power. Its members typically hold immense wealth passed between generations, and before the 20th century the emphasis fell on inherited [[Nobility|noble status]] rather than recent wealth. Because the upper classes may no longer rule the society they live in, they are often called the old upper classes and are culturally distinct from the newly rich [[Middle class|middle classes]] that tend to dominate public life in modern social democracies. In some cultures, members did not need to work, living on earned or inherited investments, often in [[Real estate|real estate]]. In [[Great Britain|Britain]] and Ireland, the class traditionally comprised landed gentry and titled aristocracy. In the [[United States]], it is estimated at less than 1% of the population, and its members derive large incomes from wealth.

Major [[Sumer|Sumerian]] city-state in ancient [[Mesopotamia]], at the site of modern Tell el-Muqayyar in Dhi Qar Governorate, [[Iraq]]. It was once a coastal city near the mouth of the [[Euphrates]] on the [[Persian Gulf]], but the shoreline has shifted and the site is now inland. Its patron was the moon god Nanna, whose shrine stood in the [[Ziggurat of Ur|ziggurat]] built in the 21st century BC under Ur-Nammu. Its Royal Tombs, dating to about the 25th or 24th century BC, held luxury items imported from Afghanistan, India and the Levant. [[Enheduanna]], appointed high priestess of Nanna by [[Sargon of Akkad]], is the potential first identifiable author in world history, though scholars are unsure whether she wrote her hymns herself.

Mountain range in [[Eurasia]] running north to south, mostly through [[Russia]], from the coast of the [[Arctic Ocean]] to the [[Ural (river)|Ural River]] in northwestern [[Kazakhstan]]. It forms part of the conventional boundary between [[Europe]] and [[Asia]], separating European Russia from [[Siberia]]. Its average altitudes are about 1,000 to 1,300 meters, and the highest point is Mount Narodnaya at 1,895 meters (6,217 feet). Its resources include metal ores, coal and precious stones, and since the 18th century they have underpinned Russia's mineral sector and heavy industry. The name Ural may derive from a Turkic term meaning stone belt. The first Russian mention came in 1096 in the Primary Chronicle.

River flowing through [[Russia]] and [[Kazakhstan]] on the continental border between [[Europe]] and [[Asia]]. It rises in the southern [[Ural Mountains]] and reaches the [[Caspian Sea]] after 2,428 kilometers (1,509 miles). At this length it is the third-longest river in Europe, after the Volga and the Danube, and the 18th-longest in Asia. It flows through Magnitogorsk, Orsk and Orenburg, then across a broad flat plain to a tree-like delta near Atyrau on the Caspian. Saray-Jük, on the river, was a Silk Road trade center that became a stronghold of the [[Golden Horde]] and was destroyed by [[Timur]] in 1395. The river was known as the Yaik until 1775, when Catherine II renamed it Ural.

Language family native to northern [[Eurasia]]. Hungarian, Finnish and Estonian have the most native speakers, and Erzya, Moksha, Mari, Udmurt and Komi each have over 100,000 speakers in European Russia. Smaller groups include the Sámi of northern Fennoscandia, Finnic languages such as Karelian, Samoyedic languages, and Mansi and Khanty of western [[Siberia]]. The name refers to a proposed original homeland near the [[Ural Mountains]], first suggested in 1823. Many languages have large case systems (Finnish has 15) and vowel harmony, and many are agglutinative, stringing [[Morpheme|morphemes]] together to form words. Proposed homelands range from the [[Volga]] region to Siberia. The earliest plausible mention of a Uralic-speaking people is in [[Tacitus]]'s *Germania*, around AD 98.

Isotope of uranium making up about 0.72% of natural uranium and the only fissile isotope that occurs in nature as a primordial nuclide. Unlike uranium-238, it can sustain a nuclear chain reaction, which powers most [[Nuclear reactor|reactors]] and [[Nuclear weapon|weapons]]. Because natural uranium contains little of it, many reactors and weapons require enriched fuel. Uranium-235 has a [[Half-life|half-life]] of 704 million years. Each fission releases an average of 2.43 [[Neutron|neutrons]], and control rods containing [[Boron|boron]], [[Cadmium|cadmium]] or [[Hafnium|hafnium]] absorb them to regulate reactor power. Arthur Jeffrey Dempster discovered it in 1935.

Chemical element with symbol U and atomic number 92, a silvery-grey metal in the [[Actinide|actinide]] series. Uranium-238 makes up over 99% of the element on Earth, while the fissile [[Uranium-235|uranium-235]] is far rarer. Uranium has the highest atomic weight of the naturally occurring elements, and it is about 70% denser than [[Lead|lead]]. Uranium was named after the planet [[Uranus]] by Martin Heinrich Klaproth in 1789, and its radioactivity was discovered by [[Henri Becquerel]] in 1896. The [[Cold War]] arms race produced tens of thousands of [[Nuclear weapon|nuclear weapons]] that used uranium metal and plutonium-239. Uranium's primary civilian use is generating electricity in [[Nuclear reactor|nuclear reactors]]. Depleted uranium is used in kinetic energy penetrators and armor plating.
